tips.title: Why she's not herself — and what that asks of you
tips.content: By the end of pregnancy, her estrogen is up roughly 100x, her cortisol triples, and her brain is being rewired in real time. The mood swings aren't a choice — they're chemistry. What that asks of you is the part nobody tells you.
paragraphs: There's a moment, usually somewhere in the first trimester, when you realize the woman you live with is not the woman you've been living with. She cries at a commercial for car insurance. She loses her temper over a dish you didn't load right. She can't decide what she wants for dinner and resents you for asking. None of it adds up — until you start understanding what her body is actually doing.

By the end of pregnancy, her estrogen is roughly a hundred times its pre-pregnancy level. Progesterone is up about tenfold. Cortisol — the body's stress hormone — roughly triples by the third trimester. These aren't background numbers. Estrogen and progesterone act directly on the brain regions that regulate mood, anxiety, and sleep. The changes you're seeing in her aren't a personality shift; they're a hormonal weather system, and she's standing in it. Knowing that doesn't make it easier to live with. But it does change the question you're answering, from 'why is she like this' to 'what's the kindest thing I can do given that she can't control this.'

The shape of it shifts by trimester. The first is usually the hardest — nausea, exhaustion, the fastest hormonal ramp, and a fear of telling anyone yet. The second is often called the honeymoon: energy returns, the worst nausea fades, and there's a window where she feels more like herself. The third is its own creature — the body is heavy, sleep is broken, and a low hum of anxiety about labor sits underneath everything. If you're calibrating expectations only off the one trimester you've seen, you'll be wrong about the next one. Watch for the change.

Here is the line you must never say, in any form: 'It's just hormones.' Or 'You're overreacting.' Or 'Calm down.' Each of those tells her that the thing happening to her isn't real, and that the person she most wants to be on her side is calling her irrational. Even when you're right — even when, technically, the snap was hormonal and the upset was disproportionate — saying so makes her more alone. The fact of the cause doesn't change the reality of the feeling. Acknowledging it is free. Withholding the acknowledgment costs you both.

What she actually needs from you, in the worst of those moments, isn't agreement and isn't argument. It's something like: 'I've got this — go rest.' Or: 'That sounded harder than it should have been. What can I take off your plate?' Or just an arm around her shoulder and your whole attention for ninety seconds. You're not fixing the chemistry. You're not winning the moment. You're being the soft place she lands in a body that, for nine months, refuses to be soft for her. Do that often enough and something quiet builds underneath the chaos: the conviction, on her side, that the man she chose to do this with actually understood what he was signing up for.
tips.pullQuote: When she snaps at something small, she's not choosing it. Her cortisol is at three times its normal level, her back is in revolt, and her brain is being rewired in real time.

tips.title: Listening when there's nothing to fix
tips.content: She doesn't always need an answer. Most of what gets called listening is actually waiting for your turn to speak. The discipline of real listening is harder — and quieter — than it looks.
paragraphs: There's a male instinct, deep and well-meaning, to hear a problem and reach for a solution. She tells you about something that hurt; you offer the next step. She names a fear; you offer reassurance. She mentions a frustration; you point out the workaround. None of that is wrong, exactly. Most of the time, in the rest of your life, it's what people are paying you for. But in the conversations that matter most during pregnancy, the move that should be your default is the one that's never been your default before: don't pivot. Don't fix. Don't reassure. Stay.

What you're learning to do is called reflective listening, and the skill at the center of it is reflecting emotion instead of words. When she says 'I'm so exhausted and I still have months to go,' the surface offering is something like 'I know, you're so close.' That's reassurance, and it lands like cardboard. The reflective offering is something like: 'It sounds like you're feeling completely drained, and it's hard to imagine keeping this up.' You haven't fixed the exhaustion. You haven't promised anything. You've shown her, with one sentence, that the thing happening inside her registered cleanly with the person across from her. That's the part she's been missing.

Then comes the move most men never make. After you reflect, instead of pivoting to logistics or pep talk, you ask one open question that goes deeper. 'What's been the hardest part of this week?' Or: 'When did it start feeling like this?' Or, simplest: 'Tell me more.' Most conversations she's been having about her pregnancy have been with people trying to be helpful — coworkers, in-laws, a doctor on a clock. Helpful is not the same as understood. Helpful asks closing questions. Understanding asks opening ones. Be the person in her week who asks the opening one.

It also helps to have a small set of phrases you can reach for when you're not sure what to say. Carry these: 'I hear you — this is real and it matters.' 'How are you, really?' 'You don't have to explain. I believe you.' 'You know what you're doing — I trust you.' 'What do you need from me right now?' Use them deliberately and they will, over time, train your voice to find them on its own. And carry the list of what to never say: 'It could be worse.' 'At least…' 'My friend's wife had it way harder.' Each of those is a silver lining built out of someone else's pain, and it makes her smaller, not lighter.

The reason any of this matters has nothing to do with being a good listener for its own sake. The trust that gets built in these small evening conversations — when she's tired, half-undressed, telling you about something that, at first glance, doesn't seem important — is the same trust she'll need to draw on when labor starts and the room is loud and a doctor she's never met is suggesting something she doesn't fully understand. The quiet moments are the deposit. The loud moments are the withdrawal. Listen now, and there will be something there for her to lean against later.
tips.pullQuote: The most powerful thing you can say in a hard conversation isn't a fix or a reassurance. It's: 'I hear you. This is real and it matters.'

tips.title: The language of her body, the language of her self
tips.content: Pregnancy stretches a woman's body faster than her sense of self can keep up. The words you use about who she is — and who she still is — change what she can carry.
paragraphs: Something happens to a woman's relationship with her own body during pregnancy that men, by default, don't have a frame for. Her body changes faster than her sense of self can keep up. Her clothes stop fitting. She catches her reflection in a window and doesn't quite recognize the silhouette. Strangers comment, in-laws comment, the internet has opinions. By the third trimester, her own mirror has become an unreliable narrator. In that climate, the words you use about her body — and about her — get amplified. They are loud whether you mean them to be or not. So choose them on purpose.

Start with one small distinction that does an enormous amount of work: 'are' versus 'look.' 'You look beautiful' is appearance-bound; it depends on the angle, the light, whether her hair is doing the thing today. 'You are beautiful' is identity-bound; it speaks to the person she is, independent of the body's current configuration. Both sentences are kind. But during a year when her body is in motion every week, the 'are' sentence is the one that holds. Pair it, when you can, with something specific: 'You are beautiful, and I am amazed by what your body is doing right now.' Now you have given her two things — that she is, and that what she is doing is being seen.

There is also a list of sentences you must never say, even in their most well-meaning forms. 'You're so big!' 'You look like you're ready to pop!' 'Wow, the baby has dropped, hasn't he.' Even when said with affection, even when she half-jokes back, those land somewhere private and they stay. Don't compare her to other pregnant women, in either direction. When she comes out of the closet half-dressed and says 'nothing fits anymore,' she is not asking for problem-solving and she is not asking for reassurance about the bump. She is asking, quietly, whether she is still attractive to you in a body she barely recognizes. The right answer isn't in your head; it's in your face and in your hands. 'You are beautiful,' you say, and you mean it. 'I know this part is hard. Want me to help you find something that feels good?' Then help her, without rushing.

The other thing she will need from you, more than anything you might guess, is the conviction that you still see her as a person whose life is bigger than this pregnancy. Most of the conversations directed at her right now are about the baby. How is the baby moving. How is the baby measuring. Have they picked a name. Sweet, all of it, and exhausting after a while. So ask her about her. About the project at work. About the book she has open on the nightstand. About the friend whose drama she was just starting to tell you about three weeks ago. Pregnancy is something she is doing; it is not the only thing she is. The man who keeps remembering that, in small ways, every week, is the man she comes out of pregnancy still feeling married to.

These are not big gestures. They are, mostly, single sentences chosen carefully and offered freely. But put together, across forty weeks, they build something durable: a sense, on her side, that the body changing in front of you and the woman inside it are both being seen, both being held, and both still belong to a life that the two of you are still living together.
tips.pullQuote: 'You are beautiful' speaks to who she is. 'You look beautiful' speaks to how she looks today. One of those holds; the other expires.

tips.title: Hard conversations, kept whole
tips.content: The hardest conversations of your marriage are the ones you're going to start having now. There is a small, learnable skill set that decides whether they end with you closer or farther apart.
paragraphs: The hardest conversations of your marriage are the ones you're about to start having. Money you've never had to plan together at this scale. Sleep no one is getting. In-laws with opinions. Birth plans with consequences. Names that one of you loves and the other one quietly hates. Pregnancy doesn't invent these tensions; it concentrates them. The good news is that the difference between a couple who comes through this stronger and a couple who comes through it bruised is not whether they fight. It's how they fight. And there's a small, learnable skill set that decides most of it.

Start with what's called the soft start-up. Years of relationship research, most famously from the Gottmans, have shown that how a conversation begins predicts roughly the shape of its entire arc. The hard version starts with 'You always' or 'You never' — sentences that catalog what the other person did wrong and put them on the defensive before the conversation has begun. The soft version starts with how you feel. 'I feel anxious about our finances' is a different doorway than 'You spend too much.' Same underlying concern, completely different room you're walking her into. Open with 'I feel,' name the situation specifically, and ask for what you need. 'I feel anxious about how fast our savings are going down. Can we sit down on Sunday and look at the next three months together?' That conversation is going to go somewhere useful. The other one isn't.

The second skill is repair. Even with the softest start-up in the world, conversations sometimes drift. Voices get sharper, someone says something they didn't mean to, the thread you started on is suddenly tangled with three others. The couples who do well aren't the couples who never get there; they're the couples who can get out. Repair attempts are the small sentences that pull the conversation back. 'I think we got off track. Can we start over?' 'I'm sorry — that came out wrong. What I meant was…' 'Hold on. I want to hear what you just said. Can you tell me again?' Said early, said often, repair is more powerful than any clever argument. It tells her that the relationship matters more to you than being right, and she needs to hear that more than she needs your point.

The third domain is money, because money during pregnancy is its own creature. The mistake most couples make is framing it as a problem with two sides — you on one, her on the other. The reframe is to put the problem on a third chair across from both of you. 'We have a problem' is adversarial; 'let's figure this out together' is shoulder-to-shoulder. When the worry is big — insurance, leave, daycare, the cost of birth itself — break it into one small action a week. You research one thing; she researches another; you compare notes Sunday night. Worry that becomes a project stops feeling like a fight and starts feeling like teamwork. That, more than any spreadsheet, is what protects a marriage from money.

The principle underneath all three skills is the same. You are not trying to win these conversations. You are trying to come out the other side still on the same team. The version of you who learns, this year, how to start soft, repair early, and frame money as a thing you do with her instead of against her — that is the version of you who, ten years from now, will have a marriage worth coming home to. Pregnancy is the practice ground. The stakes only go up from here.
tips.pullQuote: How a conversation begins predicts most of how it ends. Start with how you feel, not with what she did.

tips.title: The small things that hold you together
tips.content: Marriages aren't held together by anniversary trips. They're held together by what you do, in small ways, on the ordinary Tuesdays in between.
paragraphs: There's a particular trap first-time dads fall into in pregnancy, especially the kind of dad who wants to do this well: he assumes that the work is in the big moments. The babymoon. The push present. The proposal-style nursery reveal. He plans something grand, executes it, gets a photo, and exhales — and somewhere in the back of his head he thinks the deposit has been made. It hasn't. The truth, almost the opposite of the instinct, is that the things that actually hold a marriage together through pregnancy are small, repeatable, and almost embarrassingly mundane. They are the cup of tea on a Tuesday. They are not the trip to Mexico.

Start with a daily ritual. Pick one and keep it for the rest of the pregnancy. Some couples sit on the couch every evening and ask each other one question: what was the best part of your day, and what was the hardest? Some send a midday text just to say hi. Some keep a box of crackers on her nightstand because morning nausea hits before she's vertical. Whatever the gesture is, the magic is in the repetition. A tiny act, done every day, becomes the architecture of a marriage. A grand gesture every six months does not.

Add a weekly ritual on top of the daily one. Pick one hour, the same time every week, and call it the worry meeting. Make a cup of coffee. Pull out the things either of you has been turning over: a finance question, an in-law conversation, a fear about delivery, a logistical knot that's been waking one of you up. Talk it through, and leave with one piece of homework each. Next week you compare notes. The point isn't to solve everything — most of these worries are too big to solve in an hour. The point is that worry now has a time and a place to go. It doesn't have to be carried into the rest of the week. It doesn't have to ambush you in bed at 11 p.m. Containing it to its scheduled hour is half the relief.

Then there are the body rituals. Box breathing — in for four, hold for four, out for four, hold for four — is something to learn together, before a doctor appointment that's making her nervous, before a difficult call she has to make, before bed on a hard night. Do it as a pair. You need it as much as she does, and pretending otherwise leaves her doing the calming alone in a room that contains both of you. Add another small one starting around eighteen weeks: talk to the baby. Read a paragraph of whatever book you're reading. Narrate your walk to the kitchen. Sing the chorus of a song you like. Your voice is being learned, in there, weeks before the baby is in the room with you. The first time the baby is born and stops crying when you speak, the months of nightly nonsense will have been worth it.

A last note on timing. The second trimester is the easiest stretch of the year — the worst nausea is gone, the body is heavier but not yet exhausted, and the due date still feels far. Spend it on shared experiences. Take a class together. Spend a weekend on the nursery, just the two of you, with the kind of attention you usually save for vacation. Take the babymoon if you're going to take one. These aren't replacements for the daily and weekly rituals; they sit on top of them. But the second trimester is a deposit window that closes, and you will spend the things you put in it, with interest, in the postpartum months when there's nothing else left to spend.
tips.pullQuote: Grand gestures are easy. They cost a credit card, an afternoon, and a story you can tell. The hard thing — and the thing that actually holds — is the cup of tea, the same way she likes it, on a Tuesday no one will remember.

tips.title: How to actually be present during the third trimester
tips.content: By the third trimester, sleep is broken, her hips ache in ways she can't describe, and the finish line feels both close and impossibly far. What she needs from you in these final weeks is rarely heroic — it's quieter than that, and harder than it looks.
paragraphs: By the third trimester, your partner has been carrying another human for more than half a year. Her hips ache in ways she can't fully describe. Sleep has become a negotiation between her bladder, the baby's elbows, and a body that doesn't quite fit any pillow configuration she tries. The finish line feels close enough to taste and impossibly far at the same time. What she needs from you in these final weeks is rarely heroic. It's quieter than that, and harder than it looks.

Most first-time dads think being present means being available — physically in the room, ready to fetch ice water or rub a sore foot. That matters, but it's the floor, not the ceiling. The presence she actually feels is the kind that requires you to put your phone face-down on the counter when she walks in, to ask a follow-up question instead of a closing one, to stay in the conversation past the point where you would normally drift back to your own thoughts. It's attention as a gift, given on purpose, again and again.

Try this for a week: when she tells you something — about a kick that surprised her, about a coworker who said the wrong thing, about the fact that she's suddenly terrified of nothing in particular — don't fix it. Don't pivot to logistics. Don't reach for reassurance. Just stay. Reflect back what you heard. Ask her what part felt heaviest. You'll be amazed how often that's the entire conversation she needed, and how rarely she gets it from anyone else.

There will be evenings she snaps at you for something that isn't your fault, and mornings she cries about a commercial. Her hormones are doing the work of preparing her body to do something extraordinary, and the side effects are real. Your job in those moments is not to take it personally and not to pretend it isn't happening. Acknowledge it gently, give her the room she needs, and come back. Coming back is the part most men skip. It's the part that builds the trust she'll need when labor starts and the world gets loud.

And here's the quiet truth nobody tells you: the muscle you're building right now — the muscle of choosing her presence over your distractions — is the same muscle you'll need on the other side. The baby will arrive. The nights will get harder. The version of you who learned, in these final weeks, how to actually show up for the woman in front of him is the version of you who will know how to show up for the family you're about to have. Start now. It compounds.
tips.pullQuote: Presence isn't a single grand gesture — it's the small, repeatable act of choosing her over your phone, your inbox, your endless scroll.

tips.title: The actual cost of having a baby
tips.content: Somewhere in the second trimester the question shows up at 3 a.m.: how much is this going to cost. The headline number is real, and also misleading. Almost all the leverage you have on this bill exists before the birth, not after.
paragraphs: Somewhere in the second trimester, usually after a doctor visit you couldn't quite hear all of, a particular question shows up at three in the morning: how much is this going to cost. It hangs there, unasked at the kitchen table because asking it sounds unromantic, until you finally search it on your phone and the headline number — about twenty thousand dollars for an average pregnancy and delivery — flashes up and you wish you hadn't looked. That number is real, and also misleading. It's the total billable cost. It is not, for most families, what you'll actually pay.

With employer-sponsored insurance, the average family pays around $2,700 out of pocket from the first prenatal visit through delivery. That figure is closer to your real number than the twenty-thousand one, and the difference between them is mostly the work your insurance is doing in the background. Routine prenatal care — the regular OB visits, the standard ultrasounds, the basic labs — is covered at no cost to you under the ACA. The deductible and copays you'll see are mostly tied to delivery itself, an emergency room visit if she has one, or specialty testing. The two adjustments that change the number most are whether the birth is a C-section (which adds roughly $13,000 to the total bill, though not necessarily to your share) and whether you opt in to advanced genetic testing, which can run anywhere from $400 to $2,500 depending on the panel.

Three concrete moves to make in the first trimester, before any of this gets emotional. First: confirm that your OB, the hospital they deliver at, the anesthesiologists, and the pediatrician you choose are all in your insurance network. Out-of-network charges on a delivery bill are the single biggest source of post-birth financial shock. Second: read your plan's maternity benefits page, just once, with her, on a Sunday afternoon. Find your deductible, your out-of-pocket maximum, and your specific coverage for genetic testing. Third: call your OB's billing office and ask for a cost estimate for a vaginal birth and a C-section under your plan. Most billing offices will give you a number. That number isn't a contract, but it gives you a real range to plan against, instead of guessing against the headline figure on the internet.

The other thing nobody tells you is what shows up after. Hospital bills for births are notoriously messy — by some estimates, eighty percent of medical bills contain errors. Duplicate charges. Services billed under the wrong code. Things you did not actually receive. The version of you who gets the bill in the mail and pays it without reading it is the version of you who gives the hospital, on average, several hundred extra dollars. Don't be that version. The first move when the bill arrives is to call the billing office and ask for an itemized statement — the line-by-line list of every charge. Read it. Question anything that doesn't make sense. Then ask, plainly, whether the hospital has financial assistance or charity care programs, and whether the bill qualifies for negotiation. Many do. Even families who don't formally qualify for assistance can often get a 10-30% reduction simply by asking, especially if you can pay a smaller amount in a single check. None of this is sketchy. It's how the system works for the people who know to use it.

The fear behind the cost question is rarely the cost itself. It's the sense that the financial side of having a baby is a black box that opens after the birth, while you're already exhausted, with a number in it that you don't get to negotiate. The truth is the opposite. Almost all of the leverage you have on this bill exists in the months before delivery, when nobody is asking you to make decisions under pressure. Spend an evening on it now. Make the calls. Read the page. The version of you who walks into the hospital already knowing roughly what this will cost, what's covered, and what to do about the bill on the other side — that's the version of you who gets to spend the days after birth being a father, not a finance department.
tips.pullQuote: Almost all of the leverage you have on this bill exists in the months before delivery, when nobody is asking you to make decisions under pressure. Spend an evening on it now.

tips.title: The year the system pays you back
tips.content: The calendar year your baby is born is the most tax-favored year of your adult life. Most families leave thousands on the table because nobody told them where to look — or which thirty-day windows close on you if you don't.
paragraphs: There's a small, almost embarrassing thing that's true about the year a baby is born: the tax code, which spends most of its existence quietly extracting money from you, briefly turns into something else. For one calendar year — and only if you know to ask — it begins giving money back. The amount is not symbolic. For an average middle-income family with one new child, the combined effect of a few credits and a few pre-tax accounts is somewhere between five and nine thousand dollars a year. Most families capture some of this. Almost none capture all of it. The reason is the most boring possible: nobody told them which buttons to press, and the buttons are all in different rooms.

Start with the credits, because they're the simplest. The Child Tax Credit, after the most recent revisions, returns up to $2,200 per child to families inside its income range — not as a deduction, but as a direct reduction in what you owe, dollar for dollar. If you fall inside the Earned Income Tax Credit window — phase-outs vary, but roughly under $50,000 for a one-child family filing jointly — that's another $4,328 sitting there waiting to be claimed. Neither requires any clever planning. They require filing correctly, which means using a tax preparer or software that asks the right questions. The most common way new parents lose this money is using a too-cheap filing service in the year of birth, the one year their return suddenly isn't simple. The credit is yours; you just have to claim it on the right form.

The pre-tax accounts are the lever most people don't pull. There are three worth knowing. A Healthcare FSA lets you set aside roughly $3,300 to $3,400 in pre-tax dollars to pay medical expenses — and the year you have a baby is, by some margin, the year you'll have the most medical expenses of your life. An HSA, available only if you're on a high-deductible health plan, allows up to $8,550 to $8,750 for a family, with the rare property of being triple tax-advantaged: pre-tax going in, tax-free growth, tax-free coming out for medical use. A Dependent Care FSA — separate from the healthcare one — lets you put up to $7,500 in pre-tax dollars toward childcare in 2026. The strategic move with all three is the same: max the contribution in the calendar year you actually use it. Birth is a qualifying life event, which means you can enroll or increase outside of open enrollment if you act inside the window, usually thirty days. If you miss the window, you wait a full year for the next one, which means the year of greatest expense becomes the year you contributed the least.

Underneath these moves is a question of visibility. The credits and accounts are technical, but the failure mode is almost always emotional: the new parents who lose the most money are not the ones who don't know — they're the ones who knew, then forgot, then never went back. A budgeting app is the antidote, and the choice between them matters less than the act of choosing one. YNAB rewards couples who like systems. Mint is forgiving and visual. Goodbudget runs on the envelope method for people who think in categories. Pick one that fits the way she actually thinks about money — not the way you do — because she's the one who'll be asked to use it during the months when you're both running on three hours of sleep. Set up a category called something like Pregnancy Year, and route every co-pay, every prescription, every receipt for baby gear into it. The tax software will ask you for these numbers in April. It is dramatically faster to find them in a phone app than in a year-old email folder.

The window for all of this is narrow. The credits attach to a specific tax year. The pre-tax account contributions have to happen during the calendar year, not retroactively. The qualifying-life-event enrollment closes thirty days after birth, and the version of you who tries to file the paperwork on day twenty-eight is the version of you most likely to miss something. Spend an evening on it now, in the second trimester, while you can still think in straight lines. List the credits you're eligible for. Open the pre-tax accounts you don't have. Set the contribution rate. Pick the budgeting app. None of these moves are hard in isolation. They're hard because the system that gives them to you is built out of forms, and forms are designed for people with time on their hands, which is the resource you are about to have less of than ever before.
tips.pullQuote: The window for all of this is narrow. Spend an evening on it now, in the second trimester, while you can still think in straight lines.

tips.title: Practicing on one income
tips.content: Parental leave isn't a paycheck problem — it's a runway problem. The work you do in the months before the baby arrives decides how present you get to be in the months after.
paragraphs: There's a particular surprise that hits a lot of first-time dads in the third trimester, and it's not the obvious one. It's not labor, or sleep, or how much a stroller costs. It's the gap. The number of weeks where one or both of you isn't working, and the income you've been quietly relying on for the rent and the groceries and the gym you barely use is, abruptly, half of what it was. The federal Family and Medical Leave Act gives most parents twelve weeks of job-protected leave, but unless you live in one of the thirteen states (plus DC) that have paid family leave on top of it, those weeks are unpaid. That part doesn't change. What changes is whether you've prepared for it before it arrives.

The right way to think about parental leave isn't as a paycheck problem. It's a runway problem. You're trying to land the plane gently in a window where less money is coming in than going out, and the only real way to make that landing soft is to extend the runway. The simplest, most undervalued move is to practice now. Pick a month — ideally somewhere in the second trimester — and try living on the income you'll actually have during leave. If she's the one taking unpaid leave, run the household for a month on your salary alone. If you're both reducing income, run the math on the combined number. You will not love what you find out, and that is exactly the point. The version of this problem you discover with months to spare is a different problem than the one you discover at 2 a.m. with a newborn in the room. Find out what breaks before you can't afford for it to break.

Most households have more slack than they think they do, and almost none of it is in the dramatic places. Start with subscriptions: the average household now spends about sixty-nine dollars a month on streaming services alone, and most of that is on platforms nobody can name. Audit them. Cut the ones you've watched twice this year. Then look at dining out — typically the second-largest source of recoverable cash for a couple in their thirties — where cutting in half (not eliminating) tends to free up two to four hundred dollars a month. If you're carrying high-interest debt, attack it before the baby arrives, not after; nothing about new-parent life makes that fight easier. None of these moves are about deprivation. They're about clearing the decks for the season when you actually need the money to be there.

Underneath the runway, build a cushion. The reason this matters more than it sounds: in surveys, nearly nine in ten new mothers report that financial stress directly affects their mental health postpartum. The cushion isn't just for emergencies in the medical sense; it's for the kind of background stress that, unaddressed, leaks into every other room of postpartum life. The shape varies — some advisors say six months of post-baby living expenses, some say three, the right answer depends on your industry and your debts — but the principle is constant: there should be a number in a high-yield savings account that exists for the express purpose of not asking you any questions. Set up an automatic transfer the day after every paycheck. Even fifty dollars a month, started early, compounds in the way that matters: you build the habit while the stakes are still small, so the habit is already there when the stakes get real. While you're at it, look at short-term disability insurance — many employers offer it, often with low premiums, and it's the standard way mothers cover the unpaid portion of leave. If she has it, confirm her coverage now. If she doesn't, look at whether it's still possible to enroll. The cost of finding out is zero. The cost of needing it and not having it is the entire problem you're trying to avoid.

One last note that goes unmentioned in most dad-finance content because it doesn't sound flattering: there are government programs designed for exactly this season, and many families who qualify never check. WIC provides nutrition support during pregnancy and for children under five. CHIP covers kids in families whose income is too high for Medicaid but still inside its window. In many states, Medicaid covers pregnancy itself at income limits significantly higher than the regular threshold. None of these programs are charity in any meaningful sense — they exist because someone, decades ago, decided this was the season of life worth subsidizing. If you're inside the income lines, take the help. The whole point of having built the runway is to land the plane. The whole point of the help is to keep the landing soft. The fact that the financial side of having a baby is the hardest financial year most couples ever have is not a private failing. It's just the math. Plan against it now, take what's yours, and the season passes without leaving a mark you'll still feel five years later.
tips.pullQuote: The simplest test of whether you can afford the leave you want is whether you can live, today, on the income you'll have during it. Run the test now. Find out what breaks before you can't afford for it to break.

tips.title: The conversation nobody wants to have
tips.content: Term life insurance and a will with guardianship are the two documents that decide what happens if you're not there. Both are cheap. Most new dads don't have either, and the reason is almost never money.
paragraphs: There is a particular conversation that almost every couple expecting a child knows they need to have, and almost every couple expecting a child does not, in fact, have. It's about what happens if one of you isn't there. It sounds morbid in a way that having a baby is meant not to be, and so it gets postponed — first until after the baby shower, then until after the birth, then until after she goes back to work, and then it just sits there, indefinitely, in the category of things you'll do when life calms down, which is a category that no longer exists. The cost of having the conversation is uncomfortable. The cost of not having it is, in the literal sense, your child's future being decided by someone who has never met your family.

Term life insurance is the single most undervalued financial product available to new parents, mostly because the entire industry around it is structured to convince you to buy something else. A healthy thirty-year-old can buy $500,000 of twenty-year term coverage for somewhere between twenty-three and thirty dollars a month — about the cost of two coffees a week. The same person being sold whole life insurance, which bundles coverage with a savings vehicle nobody actually needs, is typically quoted ten to fifteen times that premium for the same coverage. Term is the one to buy. The standard sizing rule is the DIME method: add up your Debt, ten years of Income replacement, the remaining balance on your Mortgage, and the projected cost of Education, and you get a coverage number that survives most ordinary scenarios. Get quotes from at least three providers — they vary more than they should — and lock the rate while you're young, healthy, and the underwriting is friendliest.

The other document is the one almost nobody has, including, statistically, you. A will with a guardianship designation is the most important piece of paper a new parent owns, and the reason is not subtle: in the absence of one, the question of who raises your child if both parents die is decided by a probate court judge, working from a default order of relatives that may or may not match anyone's wishes. The court is not malicious. It's just a court. It picks from the available adults using rules that were not written with your particular brother-in-law in mind. The will is how you take that decision back. Naming a guardian is the part that takes the longest, not because it's legally complex, but because you have to actually decide, with her, who that person is — which is a conversation that opens up other conversations, and which is exactly why the will so often ends up unwritten.

A will alone is the floor. The rest of the package — a durable power of attorney, a healthcare directive, beneficiary designations on every account — is what keeps the floor from turning into the ceiling. The power of attorney lets someone you trust handle finances if you're incapacitated. The healthcare directive tells doctors what to do when you can't tell them yourself. Beneficiary designations override the will on retirement accounts and life insurance policies, which is why the most common will-related mistake is leaving an old girlfriend as the beneficiary on a 401(k) you opened in 2014. A basic attorney-drafted package — will, power of attorney, healthcare directive, beneficiary review — costs roughly $1,000 to $2,000 for a couple in most states. There are online services for less; for a family with a house and a kid, an attorney is the version that's harder to undo later. The single evening you spend on this is the evening you stop carrying it around.

The reason this particular conversation is the hardest one is that you have to imagine yourself, briefly, as not being there. That's the move that sticks. But the structure of the conversation, once you have it, is what dissolves the dread: the documents exist precisely so that you don't have to keep imagining it. They're the version of the worry that lives on a shelf, in a folder, instead of in your head, at three in the morning, in an apartment that contains a person who didn't exist last year. Sit down with her on a weekend. Make the calls. Sign the papers. The version of you who does this is the version of you who gets to spend the rest of fatherhood not thinking about it.
tips.pullQuote: The documents exist precisely so that you don't have to keep imagining it. They're the version of the worry that lives on a shelf, in a folder, instead of in your head, at three in the morning.

tips.title: The first month, the first year, the first eighteen
tips.content: The most consequential financial decisions of fatherhood happen across three time horizons that all open in the same week: the thirty-day paperwork window, the twelve-month childcare runway, and the eighteen-year arc you start funding now or never quite catch up on.
paragraphs: The thing nobody warns you about the first weeks of fatherhood is how much of it is paperwork. Not metaphorical paperwork. Actual paper. Forms with deadlines, in envelopes, sitting in a hospital gift bag, while you are trying to figure out how to put a car seat in a car. There is a particular kind of exhaustion that comes from being the one person in the household who is not recovering from childbirth, and there is a particular kind of unfairness in the fact that this is also the person who is supposed to handle the bureaucracy. The good news is the list of things that have to be done is short. The bad news is the deadlines are real, and the cost of missing them is mostly invisible until much later, which is exactly when you cannot afford to discover it.

There is a window. It opens at birth and it closes at thirty days, and inside it sit five things that are not optional. Add the baby to your health insurance — if you miss this, the baby is uninsured between the day they were born and the day of the next open enrollment, which depending on the calendar can be most of a year. Apply for the Social Security number at the hospital before discharge, because the alternative is a separate trip to a federal office with a newborn in a car seat. Update your W-4 to reflect the new dependent — not doing this means you over-withhold for the rest of the year, lending the IRS money you'd rather have in your account. Enroll in or increase a Dependent Care FSA, which is a benefit only available because birth is a qualifying life event, and which disappears once the window closes. And request an itemized hospital bill — not the summary, the line-by-line one — because the summary is where the billing errors hide. Set a single calendar reminder for day twenty-five. That gives you five days of slack against a thirty-day deadline, which is exactly the right amount of slack for a household running on four hours of sleep.

Past the first month, the next horizon opens, and the dominant feature of it is the cost of childcare. The numbers are larger than most expecting parents are prepared for, and they vary in a way that doesn't always match instinct. A center-based daycare averages $17,836 per year nationally, with coastal cities running well past that. An in-home daycare — a smaller operation, often run out of someone's house with a state license — runs $6,500 to $12,000, and is frequently the underrated middle ground. A nanny averages around $43,000, plus payroll taxes; an au pair, $18,200 to $27,000, plus the structural complexity of housing another adult. The decision matters less than the timing of the decision. Most well-rated daycares have waitlists of six to twelve months, which means the parents who tour facilities in the second trimester are the parents who get to choose. The parents who start the search at month seven are the parents who take whatever's left. Start touring in the third trimester if you can, even if you have no intention of deciding yet. The information you gather will compound.

The third horizon is the longest one, and the one that almost never gets attended to in the season when it matters most: the eighteen-year window between birth and college. A 529 plan is the standard vehicle, and the math is uncharitable to anyone who waits. Two hundred dollars a month, contributed from the month of birth, compounds at a roughly seven percent return into about $86,000 by the time the child is eighteen. The same contribution started at age five lands closer to $52,000. The same contribution started at age ten lands closer to $26,000. There is no investment available to a normal-income family with that kind of leverage on early action, and it costs nothing to set up. Many states layer a state tax deduction on top of the contributions, which makes the effective return higher than the headline number. Open the account at month one. Set up an automatic transfer of whatever you can sustain — a hundred dollars, fifty, twenty if that's what fits — and the habit will be there long before the stakes are.

The reason these three horizons sit in the same article is that they all open in the same week. The first month is reaction. The first year is logistics. The first eighteen years is faith — or, more precisely, faith expressed through a recurring transfer that started when the child was a week old. Most fathers manage one of the three. A few manage two. Almost none manage all three, and the reason is not money. It's that the season in which all three become possible is the season in which you have the least bandwidth to think about any of them. The trick, if there is one, is to do as much of it as you can before the baby actually arrives — schedule the calendar reminders, tour the daycares, open the 529 account empty — so that the version of you living on broken sleep is doing execution, not decisions. The decisions are easier now. Make them now.
tips.pullQuote: The first month is reaction. The first year is logistics. The first eighteen years is faith — or, more precisely, faith expressed through a recurring transfer that started when the child was a week old.

tips.title: The four things you don't compromise on
tips.content: Most of what gets sold to first-time parents is fashion. A small number of items aren't — and one of them has a federal regulation closing in December 2026 that almost nobody is talking about.
paragraphs: The baby aisle at any big-box store is overwhelming on purpose. Most of what's there can be bought new, used, borrowed, or skipped without consequence — and most of what gets opinionated about online (the brand of stroller, the fabric of the swaddle, the right white-noise machine) lives entirely in that fungible majority. There's a much smaller list — four items, more or less — where the choice actually matters. They're the ones where a hundred-dollar mistake becomes a several-thousand-dollar mistake, or worse. The exhausting part of preparing for a baby isn't researching the gear. It's separating that small list from the noise around it, and handling it deliberately, before the noise wins.

Start with the car seat, because it's the only piece of baby gear with a federal regulation about to change underneath it. FMVSS 213b — the updated federal standard with new side-impact testing — becomes mandatory in December 2026. Anything sold after that date will meet it; anything sold before may or may not, depending on the manufacturer. If you're buying a seat in 2026, ask whether the model has been certified to 213b, not just to the older 213. There's a second decision underneath that one: infant bucket seat or convertible. The bucket — the click-in, click-out kind that doubles as a carrier — is convenient for the first few months and outgrown in 6 to 18. The convertible costs more upfront and lasts 3 to 10 years, which is the better math for most families who don't already have a bucket from a sibling. Either way: install rear-facing, install by week 36, and have it inspected at a certified inspection station. The seat is one of the few products in your house where 'mostly correct' and 'correct' have very different consequences.

The second item is the crib. Not the frame — the frame is fashion — but what goes in it. The mattress must be new, firm, and flat. Used mattresses are the one item where secondhand is an actual safety problem: foams degrade, fluids penetrate in ways that don't always show on the surface, and the firmness rating can decay invisibly. Inside the crib, nothing else: no bumpers (now banned), no blankets, no pillows, no stuffed animals, no positioners. A fitted sheet is the entire ensemble. Keep the room between 68 and 72 degrees, and room-share — same room, not the same bed — for at least the first six months. The point of all of this isn't aesthetic minimalism. It's that the conditions known to reduce SIDS risk are unfashionably specific, and the parents who improvise on them are mostly improvising against a number they haven't seen.

The third item is the carrier, which most dads underestimate because it looks like a fabric accessory. It isn't. A carrier worn wrong puts the baby in the wrong position for breathing or hip development; worn right, it's the thing that gives you back your hands for the first months of the baby's life. The five-rule version of 'worn right' is the T.I.C.K.S. checklist, written down by babywearing safety bodies: Tight enough that the baby can't slump; In view at all times; Close enough to kiss the top of the head; Keep chin off chest; Supported back, with the spine in its natural curve. Try a few styles — a stretchy wrap, a structured carrier, a ring sling — because they fit different bodies differently and the right one is mostly the one you'll actually use. The fourth item is the system around the car seat: the car itself. By week 36, install the seat and have it inspected. From that week forward, keep the gas tank at least half full, because labor doesn't time itself to your fuel light. Toss a small kit in the trunk — a blanket, a flashlight, a couple bottles of water — and the version of you who needs it never has to think about it.

The reason these four sit together is that they share a property the rest of the baby aisle doesn't: getting them right is invisible, and getting them wrong shows up later, often quietly, often in places you can't undo. Everything else — the bouncer, the swing, the third-tier stroller, the dresser with the changing pad on top — can be bought new, used, late, or never, and the worst case is mild inconvenience. The car seat that meets the new standard, the bare crib, the carrier worn the way the safety bodies wrote it down, and the car ready to leave at 2 a.m. — those four are the ones that quietly carry the rest of it. Handle them in the second trimester, while you can still think in straight lines, and you'll spend the third trimester worrying about smaller things, which is the version of the third trimester you want.
tips.pullQuote: The car seat that meets the new standard, the bare crib, the carrier worn right, and the car ready to leave at 2 a.m. — those four are the ones that quietly carry the rest of it.

tips.title: What to ask for, what to ignore, what to inherit
tips.content: A baby registry isn't a wishlist. It's the only window in the run-up to a baby where a lot of money is about to be spent on you, and you have a small amount of control over where it goes. Done well, it does three jobs at once.
paragraphs: The registry shows up in the second trimester as a kind of Pinterest board with prices, and two hours into building one you realize it's actually doing something stranger. It's the only window in the run-up to a baby where a lot of money is about to be spent on you, and you have a small amount of control over where it goes. Most first-time parents treat it like a wishlist. The couples who get the most out of it treat it like a strategy document. The strategy is built from three lists, and the trick is knowing which item belongs on which.

List one is what to ask for. The principle is to load the registry with essentials at every price point — small items (bottles, swaddles, sleep sacks), mid items (a monitor, a carrier, a bouncer), and a few large items that the right relative might pick up alone or in a group (the stroller, the car seat, the convertible crib). List two to three times more items than guests, because items get bought in unpredictable orders and an empty registry late in the third trimester is the version of this where you end up at Target on a Saturday at 35 weeks. Use a universal registry platform that pulls from multiple stores rather than locking yourself into one — guests don't notice the difference, but it widens what's available and stacks better with completion discounts. Speaking of which: Amazon, for example, offers Prime members 15% off the remaining items near the end of the registry window. Wait until the shower is over to buy what's left, and you'll save more than you'd guess.

List two is what to leave off. Most of what gets marketed hardest to expecting parents is, on close inspection, solving a problem they don't actually have. Wipe warmers exist because someone decided room-temperature wipes were an emergency; they aren't. Newborn shoes are sold for babies who, by definition, won't be walking for the better part of a year. Car seat mirrors look reassuring but distract drivers in a way the safety community has been warning about for two decades. Wearable baby monitors — the sock that tracks oxygen and pulse — look like data and turn out to be a generator of 3 a.m. anxiety calls about readings that mean nothing. Bottle sterilizers replace a dishwasher that already sterilizes. Crib bumpers are simply banned. None of these is going to ruin your life if it ends up in your house. But each of them takes a slot on a registry that could've been a sleep sack instead.

List three is the longest, and the one that saves the most money: what to buy used or borrow. The baby gear secondhand market is one of the most dramatically discounted in any consumer category, because the items are outgrown so fast that resale is mostly a question of finding someone six months ahead of you who's done. A UPPAbaby Vista that retails for $900 sells for $150 used in most cities. Baby clothes — outgrown in weeks, often worn three times — should default to hand-me-downs unless you have a specific reason. Bouncers and swings, used for a window of two to four months, are the highest-value items to borrow rather than buy. A crib frame, a dresser, a high chair (eventually), a play mat — all fine used, assuming you check cpsc.gov for recalls and the model is current. Across an average gear list, families who buy used strategically save somewhere between $1,650 and $4,000. The exception, named once and held to: car seats, crib mattresses, and bassinets are not on the used list, ever.

The mistake almost nobody making a registry sees in real time is that the three lists aren't equally weighted. The 'ask for' list is a few dozen items. The 'ignore' list saves you a few hundred dollars. The 'inherit' list saves thousands, and almost no first-time couple builds it deliberately. Most of the friends and family one or two stages ahead of you have things in their garages they would gladly send you, and they're waiting for someone to ask. So ask. Send a group text in the second trimester listing, by name, the half-dozen big-ticket items you'd take used or borrowed. The replies will surprise you. The registry is the front door of the strategy. The back door — the friend whose toddler just outgrew the bouncer, the cousin with two strollers in the basement — is where most of the math actually happens.
tips.pullQuote: Most first-time parents treat the registry like a wishlist. The couples who get the most out of it treat it like a strategy document.

tips.title: Babyproof in Phases
tips.content: Phase 1 (3rd trimester): Anchor furniture, install smoke/CO detectors, cover outlets, set water heater to 120°F, switch to cordless blinds. Phase 2 (6-12 months): Cabinet locks, stair gates, corner guards. Phase 3 (12+ months): Toilet locks, stove knob covers, window guards.

tips.title: Set Up the Nursery Wisely
tips.content: Budget nursery: $610-$1,225. Mid-range: $1,465-$2,910. A dresser with changing pad on top is more versatile than a dedicated changing table. Blackout curtains help sleep. Sound machine below 50 decibels, at least 2 feet from crib.

tips.title: Essential Clothing Needs
tips.content: You need less than you think: 6-10 onesies, 4-7 pajamas, 3-5 pants, 4-6 pairs of socks. Buy mostly 0-3 month size — newborn size is outgrown in 2-4 weeks. Buy used or accept hand-me-downs for maximum savings.

tips.title: Prepare Feeding Supplies
tips.content: Start with 4-6 bottles to test preferences before committing to a brand. Breast pumps are typically covered free by insurance under the ACA — call your insurer to order one. High chairs aren't needed until about 6 months.

tips.title: Understand Diapering Costs
tips.content: Disposable diapers cost $1,500-$3,000 from birth to potty training. Cloth diapers require $300-$600 upfront but save 30-50% overall. A contoured changing pad on a dresser is more versatile than a standalone changing table.

tips.title: Set Up Changing Stations
tips.content: Create a main changing hub in the nursery and a smaller version in a high-traffic area. For two-level homes, have one station per floor. Each needs: changing pad, diapers, wipes, diaper cream, a few changes of clothes, and disposal bags.

tips.title: Order Nursery Furniture by Week 20
tips.content: Allow 4-8 weeks for furniture delivery. New furniture should off-gas for at least 2-4 weeks before baby arrives. Convertible cribs (3-in-1 or 4-in-1) offer the best long-term value. Anchor ALL furniture to walls with anti-tip straps.

tips.title: Learn the 5-1-1 Rule
tips.content: Go to the hospital when contractions are 5 minutes apart, lasting 1 minute each, for at least 1 hour. Before that, early labor can last hours at home. Call your provider if water breaks, you see heavy bleeding, or she has severe pain between contractions.

tips.title: Know the Stages of Labor
tips.content: Stage 1: Contractions dilate the cervix (early labor 0-6cm, active labor 6-10cm). Stage 2: Pushing and delivery. Stage 3: Delivery of the placenta. Early labor is the longest — active labor typically lasts 4-8 hours for first-time moms.

tips.title: Master Comfort Measures
tips.content: Counter-pressure on the lower back during contractions, hip squeezes, massage, cool washcloths on the forehead, and guided breathing. Practice these before labor so they feel natural. Your calm presence is her most powerful pain relief tool.

tips.title: Use the BRAIN Framework
tips.content: When facing unexpected medical recommendations, ask: What are the Benefits? The Risks? The Alternatives? What does your Intuition say? What happens if we do Nothing (wait)? This helps you make decisions under pressure without feeling steamrolled.

tips.title: Pack the Hospital Bag by Week 35
tips.content: For her: personal pillow, lip balm, nursing robe, loose pants, grippy socks, breastfeeding pillow. For you: change of clothes, pillow, snacks, chargers, camera, book for early labor. For baby: going-home outfit in 2 sizes, swaddle blankets, Aquaphor.

tips.title: Understand Pain Management Options
tips.content: Epidurals offer the highest pain relief but limit mobility. Nitrous oxide provides moderate relief with good mobility. Non-pharmacological options like hydrotherapy, TENS, and hypnobirthing preserve full mobility. Discuss preferences before labor.

tips.title: Know What NOT to Say During Labor
tips.content: Don't say: 'Calm down,' 'It can't be that bad,' 'Are you sure you don't want the epidural?', or 'My feet hurt too.' Do say: 'You're doing amazing,' 'I'm right here,' 'What do you need?' Follow her lead completely.

tips.title: Prepare for a C-Section Possibility
tips.content: About 32% of US births are C-sections. Some are planned, many are emergency decisions. Know what to expect: spinal anesthesia, a curtain at chest level, you'll sit by her head, and the surgery takes about 45-60 minutes. Recovery is longer than vaginal birth.

tips.title: Choose Your Pediatrician by Week 36
tips.content: Interview pediatricians in the third trimester. Ask about after-hours availability, vaccination philosophy, and communication preferences. Many hospitals have the pediatrician visit within 24 hours of birth for the first checkup.

tips.title: Pre-Register at the Hospital
tips.content: Pre-register between weeks 20-26 to avoid paperwork during labor. Confirm insurance pre-authorization for delivery. Take a hospital tour to know the layout — where to park, where to check in, and the fastest route from your home.

tips.title: Create a Birth Plan (But Stay Flexible)
tips.content: Include preferences for pain management, delivery positions, cord cutting, skin-to-skin, and breastfeeding. But remember: a birth plan is not a contract. Unexpected events may require rapid changes. Flexibility reduces disappointment.

tips.title: Be Her Advocate in the Delivery Room
tips.content: Speak up when she can't — communicate her wishes to the medical team. Ask for explanations when procedures are recommended. Make sure she's comfortable, hydrated, and heard. You are her voice when she's focused on labor.

tips.title: Prepare 15-20 Freezer Meals
tips.content: Start meal prep around week 30. Aim for 25-50 individual portions. Best freezer meals: casseroles, soups, breakfast egg muffins, and handheld foods like burritos. Portion into 2-3 serving containers. Label everything with contents, date, and reheating instructions.

tips.title: Know the Baby Blues vs. Postpartum Depression
tips.content: Baby blues affect up to 80% of new mothers and resolve within 2 weeks — mood swings, crying, anxiety. Postpartum depression is different: persistent sadness, withdrawal, inability to sleep even when baby sleeps. If symptoms last beyond 2 weeks, seek professional help.

tips.title: Watch for Paternal Postpartum Depression
tips.content: 8-10% of fathers experience postpartum depression, peaking 3-6 months after birth. Signs: irritability, withdrawal, anger, risk-taking. Children raised by fathers with depression have higher risk of emotional difficulties. Don't hesitate to seek help — PSI Helpline: 1-800-944-4773.

tips.title: Implement Tag-Team Sleep Strategy
tips.content: Divide nighttime duties so each partner gets at least one 4-5 hour uninterrupted sleep block. Sleep deprivation affects judgment, mood, and health. This isn't about being fair — it's about keeping both parents functional and safe.

tips.title: Set Up a Visitor Policy in Advance
tips.content: Decide together: who visits, when, and for how long. Require hand-washing and current vaccinations. It's okay to say no or limit visits. Your partner needs rest and bonding time, not a parade of guests. Set boundaries early.

tips.title: Add Baby to Insurance Within 30 Days
tips.content: This is a qualifying life event — you have 30-60 days to add baby to your health insurance. Apply for the Social Security number at the hospital. Update your W-4 at work. Missing these deadlines can mean gaps in coverage.

tips.title: Learn Newborn Care Basics Before Birth
tips.content: Practice diapering, swaddling, and safe sleep positioning before the baby arrives. Learn to recognize hunger cues: rooting, hand-to-mouth, fussiness. Crying is always last — if you catch earlier cues, feeding is easier.

tips.title: Watch for Postpartum Warning Signs
tips.content: Emergency signs after birth: heavy bleeding (soaking a pad in an hour), seizures, severe headaches, vision changes, and fever over 100.4°F. Postpartum preeclampsia can occur up to 6 weeks after delivery. Know when to call 911 vs. the doctor.

tips.title: Schedule the Newborn's First Appointments
tips.content: First pediatrician visit within 3-5 days of discharge. The 6-week postpartum checkup for your partner. Newborn hearing screening and metabolic screening happen at the hospital. Keep a log of feedings, diapers, and sleep patterns.

tips.title: Maintain Your Own Self-Care
tips.content: Exercise, sleep, and social connection aren't selfish — they make you a better partner and father. Keep at least one personal hobby. Connect with other dads. You can't pour from an empty cup. Take care of yourself so you can take care of your family.
